items.title: Act and rule utilitarianism give different answers
items.claim: What is the distinction between act and rule utilitarianism?

options.text: They are alternative names for the same theory

Act utilitarianism judges each action by its consequences directly; rule utilitarianism asks which rules, if generally followed, would produce the greatest happiness — and applies those rules even when an individual act might seem to maximise utility differently
Act utilitarianism is the only legitimate form

items.reveal:
Jeremy Bentham's 'Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation' (1789) introduced the hedonic calculus. John Stuart Mill's 'Utilitarianism' (1861) distinguished higher and lower pleasures.

Rule utilitarianism (developed by R.M. Hare and Richard Brandt in the 20th century) attempts to address objections to act utilitarianism — that it permits horrific acts (killing one innocent to save five) and creates impossible decision burdens.

Critics argue rule utilitarianism collapses into act utilitarianism (just add 'except in special cases') or into Kantian deontology (just follow the rules).
items.why: Utilitarianism is not one theory. The act/rule distinction changes the answers radically — and exam answers that treat 'utilitarianism' as monolithic miss the most important internal debate.

items.title: Hindu deities are often manifestations of one ultimate reality
items.claim: How does Hindu theology relate the many gods to Brahman?

options.text: Each god is wholly separate and independent

Many Hindus understand the gods as manifestations (devas) of one ultimate reality (Brahman) — though the relationship varies between traditions, and some bhakti movements emphasise a personal supreme deity (Vishnu, Shiva, Devi)
There is only one god in Hinduism — Brahma

items.reveal:
The Rig Veda (1.164.46) says 'Truth is one; sages call it by many names.' The Trimurti (Brahma the creator, Vishnu the preserver, Shiva the destroyer) is one classical way of mapping cosmic functions.

Vaishnavism centres on Vishnu and his avatars (Rama, Krishna). Shaivism centres on Shiva. Shaktism centres on Devi/Shakti (the divine feminine, including Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati). Each tradition may treat its chosen deity as supreme.

The term 'henotheism' (worshipping one god while acknowledging others) was coined by Max Müller in the 19th century specifically to describe Vedic religion.
items.why: Calling Hinduism polytheistic or monotheistic both miss the structure. The 'many manifestations of one' framework is philosophically distinct — and shapes how Hindus actually relate to images and shrines.

items.title: Buddhism does not teach a creator god
items.claim: Does classical Buddhism teach a supreme creator deity?

options.text: Yes, the Buddha is worshipped as supreme deity
No — classical Buddhism rejects an eternal creator god; gods (devas) may exist but are themselves caught in samsara; liberation depends on the Eightfold Path, not divine grace
Yes, Brahma is the Buddhist supreme being
Only Mahayana affirms a creator god

items.reveal:
In the Pali Canon, the Buddha refuses metaphysical speculation about a creator (e.g. the Aggi-Vacchagotta Sutta, the 'parable of the poisoned arrow'). Devas exist but are impermanent and themselves seek liberation. The path to nibbana does not depend on grace from a supreme being.

Later traditions (Pure Land, some Mahayana schools) develop devotional practice toward Buddhas and bodhisattvas, but these are still not creators in the Abrahamic sense.

The Buddha is not a god — he is an awakened human teacher. Buddha statues are reminders, not objects of worship as deity.
items.why: Western definitions of religion centre on theism. Buddhism is a major world tradition that fits awkwardly inside that frame — and forces a rethink of what 'religion' even means.
